content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is a tropical fruit native to South America. It has a sweet-tart flavor, juicy fragrant flesh, and a tough, spiky skin. Pineapple is eaten fresh, canned, or as juice, and is added to desserts, salads, baked goods, and meat dishes, or grilled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A pineapple is not a single fruit but a multiple fruit formed from many fused berries.
It grows not on a tree but on a low plant close to the ground.
Pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down proteins, which is why fresh pineapple can make your mouth tingle.
Because of bromelain, gelatin made with raw pineapple does not set, while canned pineapple does not have this effect.
Pineapple does not become noticeably sweeter after harvest, so it is important to choose a ripe fruit.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains manganese
items.content: Manganese plays a role in metabolism and bone formation.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain is studied as a compound that may support digestion.

items.title: Contains fiber and water
items.content: Pineapple is refreshing and provides some fiber.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: It provides thiamine and vitamin B6, which help the body get energy from food.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Pineapple is acidic and may cause heartburn or irritate the mouth, tongue, and tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Pineapple allergy is possible, including reactions to bromelain.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Pineapple contains natural sugars, so people with diabetes should watch their portion size.

items.title: Bromelain and medications
items.content: Large amounts of bromelain or bromelain supplements may interact with anticoagulants and some antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut off the top and base, slice away the skin, remove the "eyes," and, if you like, the tough core. Cut the flesh into slices or cubes and eat it fresh, add it to salads, smoothies, yogurt, and desserts, or grill it. Choose canned pineapple in its own juice rather than in syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A whole pineapple can be kept at room temperature for one to two days, then moved to the refrigerator. Store cut pineapple in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–5 days, or freeze it in pieces. Store canned pineapple as directed on the package, and refrigerate it after opening.
